subject: turtle
pitch: A green sea turtle gliding through the water. A heart-shaped shell with olive and caramel plates traced in darker brown, a pale yellow belly plate, a blunt head with cream-edged scales, dark wise eyes and a gentle beak. Long front flippers spread wide, short rear flippers, and a little remora fish riding under its shell.
reasoning:
I'm planning a sea turtle module at realistic scale, around 1.1 meters shell length, oriented facing +Z, and thinking through how to handle the ground-placement rule for a creature that's swimming rather than standing.

I'm sketching the joint hierarchy: a body root, a neck-to-head-to-jaw chain, and front flippers built from shoulder-elbow-wrist chains with flat slab shapes for the flipper paddles, deciding to keep everything simple with sweeps and polygon slabs rather than complex geometry.

For the shell itself, I'm choosing between a scaled sphere and an extruded heart-shaped outline lying flat in the XZ plane, working out the orientation vectors needed so the extrusion's thickness runs along Y while the heart shape spans X and Z correctly.

I'm sketching the heart outline points for the carapace: a notch at the front center, rounded lobes flanking it, tapering sides, and a tapered back tip, with smoothing applied except at the sharp notch point so the shape reads as a proper turtle shell.

For the extrude axes, I'm checking the orientation vectors so the shell sits flat with correct thickness centered along its normal. For the shell texture I'm planning to use a scale pattern with olive and caramel base tones outlined in dark brown to mimic the plated look of a carapace, then considering whether to add marginal scute trim before moving on to building the plastron.

I'm positioning a smaller pale heart-shaped plastron beneath the shell, adjusting its y-offset and thickness so it slightly overlaps the shell's underside, acknowledging the turtle's body will sit hidden inside. Then I start thinking about the neck, planning to use a sweep along a path of points with a rounded capsule-like radius and olive-green color, and considering rigging it as a jointed chain for animation.

Now I'm working out the head: a blunt sphere scaled to be slightly elongated, painted olive-green with cream-colored scale edges, positioned at the end of the neck chain, plus small dark eye spheres placed symmetrically near the front of the head.

For the beak and jaw, I'm adding a jaw joint beneath the head so the mouth can hinge open, with separate upper and lower beak parts colored dark olive. Then I'm setting up shoulder joints off a central body root joint so I can build flipper chains spreading outward on each side.

Now I'm defining the arm chains as multi-point polylines from shoulder to wrist with named segments, then wrapping each with a flat flipper-shaped slab mesh using leading and trailing edge coordinates to give it a wide, paddle-like outline.

Mirroring the design for the right flipper by negating x and trusting the slab's Newell-based normal calculation to handle correct winding either way. For the rear flippers, I'm sketching a smaller paddle-shaped outline anchored to a hip joint, keeping similar polygon logic but scaled down and positioned further back on the body.

Now I'm checking ground clearance: the current lowest points (flipper undersides, plastron) sit around y=0.175–0.185, but the rule requires the lowest point to actually touch y=0. Since this is an aquatic turtle gliding through water rather than standing, I'm debating whether to force it to the floor anyway per the rules, and considering shifting the entire model down by a uniform offset so the real lowest point lands at y=0 without having to rework all the individual height values.

I'm working out the plastron and shell dimensions so the bottom rests at y=0, setting plastron center around 0.03-0.04 with thickness 0.06 so its bottom touches the floor, then placing the shell above it with its own thickness and bevel for a rounded dome. I notice there's a gap between the plastron top and shell bottom where the body should connect, so I'm considering adding a filler shape to bridge that space.

Now I'm filling that gap with an olive-green ellipsoid "torso" scaled from a sphere, positioned so it tucks neatly between the plastron and shell without poking through either, and checking that the flippers attach at a reasonable shoulder height relative to that body. I'm also sanity-checking overall proportions -- shell length around 1m, width under a meter, head sized around 0.2m -- against real green sea turtle dimensions, then starting to chain joint positions from the body front toward the neck and head.

I'm planning the neck as a three-point catmull chain with joints named neck1, neck2, and head, figuring out how the chain's tip joint lands at the path's end and how its root connects back to the body's root joint. Setting up a short tail too, then working out how to sweep a tube along the neck chain with tapering radii to form the neck geometry.

For the head I'm placing a scaled sphere at the head joint with a blunt, slightly elongated shape, painting it with a scale pattern blending two greens into a cream edge. Then I'm positioning small eye spheres on the sphere's surface using trigonometry to find the right offset coordinates, aiming for a wise expression with dark pupils and a subtle highlight.

Now I'm building the jaw joint and beak using boxes attached to the head and jaw bones, with the upper beak darker olive and lower jaw a lighter tan, adjusting positions so they sit at the front of the head sphere. Next I'm starting on the shoulder joints and flipper chains, working out coordinates for the arm bones extending outward from the body.

Defining flipper geometry...

Mirroring the flippers for the right side by negating x-coordinates, then adding rear flipper slabs attached to a hip joint near the back of the shell. I'm also setting up the shoulder joint chain for the front arm, parenting it to the body so the rigging connects properly.

Now I'm working through the remora placement — it's supposed to sit under the shell, but the plastron already occupies that lowest space near the floor, so I need to either nudge the remora's position or raise the whole turtle slightly so the remora can tuck beneath without clipping through the belly.

I'm weighing whether I can just shift the root group's position down instead of offsetting every coordinate, though I'm unsure the harness will track that properly. I think baking in a lift constant to each y-value is safer, even if more tedious, so I keep deliberating on how to apply it consistently without breaking the remora's position relative to the belly.

Now I'm trying to place the remora fish under the shell without it intersecting the torso ellipsoid — testing positions near the shell's underside edge where it would be partially tucked under the rim but still visible from the front-left.

I decide to keep the model resting on the floor with plastron bottom at 0, and instead tuck the remora along the flank, pressed against the torso surface near x=-0.32, running along the z-axis from about 0.1 to -0.3, with a tapered sweep and flattened sucker-disc head.

I work out the fuller construction plan: a tail sweep extending beneath and past the shell's rear, scale-pattern paint for the shell plates with darker outline tracing, and a heart-shaped plastron outline extruded flat in the XZ plane using proper x/y axis vectors so it lies belly-side rather than standing up like a wall. I define the shell as a similarly heart-shaped but larger outline with a front notch and tapered thickness for a dome profile, work out bevel limits, and settle the torso as a scaled ellipsoid hidden mostly inside the shell and plastron.

I then sketch out the joint hierarchy -- root body joint, neck chain leading to a head joint, a jaw joint parented to the head, and leg/arm-style flipper joints -- along with sweeps for the neck and tail with tapered radii, and reconsider the remora's sucker disc position so it doesn't clip through the shell's underside.

Writing extrude code...

Still writing flipper code...

Writing joint hierarchy...

Writing neck sweep...

Writing head and eye code...

Writing remora code...

Writing tail sweep...

Writing torso code...

I also double check the typing details -- confirming that scale and position options accept array literals correctly, that paint functions accept arrays of color strings, and that joint directions and bone bindings are valid -- before finalizing the full component and returning the built root object with its metadata export.
